title: Genomically rewritten and tailored humanized mouse models for various organ disorders
text:
An “instruction manual” on when and where genes are to be expressed can be significantly larger than gene
itself, even 100 times as big. This makes deciphering the causes of genetic disease a challenge. Our group has
developed methods to probe this “dark matter of the genome” and will use this proposal to make 16-24
mouse models of human disease susceptibility for a broad range of human diseases affecting the brain, the
eye, cardiovascular disease and the immune system.

title: Cortico-striatal mechanisms of Alcohol on E/I balance
text: P2 SUMMARY Dramatic rates of alcohol use disorder (AUD) are a major public health concern and limited treatment approaches make translational research imperative for the development of new interventions. AUD is associated with a hyper-glutamatergic state and genomic and transcriptomic data generated by CTNA5 found a disturbance in excitation-to-inhibition (E/I) balance. The identification of cell-type and circuit-specific alterations in genes implicated in glutamate and GABA synaptic transmission in individuals with AUD provides novel targets for functional studies in rodent models. Project 2 will test the overarching hypothesis of CTNA6 that altered E/I balance as a result of changes in AUD risk gene expression underlies susceptibility to increased alcohol use and seeking. CTNA5 established the role of medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC)→nucleus accumbens (NAc) circuits in habitual alcohol-seeking and decision-making dysfunctions, and also that a mGluR5 negative allosteric modulator (mavoglurant) could reduce alcohol consumption – consistent with dysregulated glutamatergic signaling. Aim 1 will determine E/I ratio and network activity changes during chronic alcohol use in mPFC→NAc circuitry using slice electrophysiology and dual color fiber photometry to dissect changes in excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission and cell-type specific neural dynamics longitudinally throughout a chronic Drinking-in-the-Dark (DID) paradigm and operant self- administration in mice. Our preliminary data support that E/I ratio in the mPFC show sex-specific changes at the end of the 4-week chronic DID. Aim 2 will investigate the role of three AUD risk genes, CACNA1C, CACNA1E, and NR3C1 in E/I regulation in alcohol-related behaviors using cell-type specific mouse models of these risk genes, and test if they are more vulnerable to develop escalated alcohol drinking and seeking. Aim 3 will assess the effects of nimodipine and topiramate on E/I ratio, alcohol consumption and alcohol-seeking behaviors. Despite known sex differences in AUD neurobiology, the interaction between sex and altered synaptic transmission and neural dynamics is not well understood and will be studied. Our work is highly integrated with CTNA6 Projects 1 & 3 that use genomic and transcriptomic approaches to identify potential therapeutic targets and use imaging assessments of hyperexcitability states in AUD, and is complementary because we can generate a level of mechanistic insight not possible from AUD data. Project 2 will permit a highly mechanistic understanding of cell-type specific information on the trajectory of E/I imbalance in cortico- striatal circuits and determine the ability of select pharmacological agents to restore altered synaptic function and network dynamics, and, to remediate alcohol consumption and seeking behavior.

title: Functional RNA elements in the human genome
text:
RNAs are bound and regulated by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), which play critical roles in RNA splicing,
subcellular localization, translation, and degradation Experimental studies and computational predictions
suggest the existence of thousands of RBPs in the human genome. Here we generate and use novel
experimental technologies, data resources and computational tools to comprehensively study the role of these
of predicted and known RBPs in RNA processing and cellular function.

title: Characterization of Whole Brain Demyelination and Axon Damage Using High-resolution Magnetic Resonance Imaging
text:
The goal of this project is to develop novel high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging
techniques to detect and monitor the demyelination and axon damage processes in both white
matter and cerebral cortex, especially in the early stage of multiple sclerosis. The successful
outcome of the proposed project will advance and benefit the understanding the complex
mechanism of multiple sclerosis and early diagnosis of the disease.

title: High Throughput Sciences
text: High Throughput Sciences Core: Project Summary/Abstract The Koch Institute High Throughput Sciences Core (HTS Core) provides automated technologies, expertise and training that allows Cancer Center Members to investigate the interplay between biomaterials, biomolecules, small molecules and cells in a high-throughput, multiplexed manner to enable drug and gene discovery, drug delivery, toxicology, and systems biology applications. The HTS Core possesses state-of-the-art robotic instrumentation, an array of biological tools, including validated cell lines and curated libraries, and an exceptional staff with expertise in assay development and adaptation, screening execution, and robotics workflows. HTS Core activities were established in 2011, with support from CCSG Developmental Funds and Institutional support. In the prior submission, HTS activities were embedded in the Koch Institute Genomics Core, reflecting their extensive interactions. During this current period, the HTS Core has greatly expanded its roles and impact for both Center Members and other Koch Institute Cores. Given this, and on the advice of our SAB, we are requesting funding for High Throughput Sciences as a stand-alone Core. In the current funding period, the HTS Core added a significant number of new capabilities and modified existing services, including: a new high throughput flow cytometer and tissue processing equipment; added >55,000 new compounds to small molecule libraries; automated workflows for ELISAs, high content imaging and HT sample preparation pipelines, including automated plate-based HT ChIP-Seq sample preparation (collaborating with the Integrated Genomics & Bioinformatics Core); and cell line management services, including mycoplasma testing and banking of mycoplasma-free cell lines. Center Member Core use has been strong: 66% of Center Members use the Core, account for 73% of Core service use, and include investigators from all three Research Programs. In the upcoming period, the HTS Core will continue to offer a wide range of state-of-the-art services to support Center Member research programs, and will evaluate emerging capabilities in the context of Center Member needs and interests. A number of new initiatives are planned, including: acquisition and evaluation of new equipment; upgrades to existing equipment; acquisition of new CRISPR and targeted small molecule libraries; establishment of small molecule screening in zebrafish; continued collaboration with other Koch Institute Core Facilities to develop technology and streamline workflows; deployment of a custom-built LIMS system to manage library materials and screening assay data; dataset sharing to support development of machine learning algorithms; and collaborating with other Koch Institute Cores to develop a monthly workshop series to support Center Members’ access to imaging technology platforms and data analysis. This Shared Resource is essential to the success of the Koch Institute mission and provides exceptional value to the CCSG. The requested CCSG budget for Year 49 is increased by 1.6% over the Core CCSG budget for the current period (Year 48).

title: Machine Learning-based Imaging Biomarkers for Metabolic and Age-related Diseases
text:
Program Director/Principal Investigator (Last, First, Middle): Makrogiannis, Sokratis
Narrative
Age-related and metabolic diseases, such as type-2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, sarcopenia,
osteoporosis, and osteoarthritis, have become a worldwide epidemic, and affect the quality of life of millions. To
give a global perspective, roughly 343.8 million people in the world have type-2 diabetes today, and 175 million
don’t know they have diabetes at all. This project will contribute novel and non-invasive medical image analysis
techniques for studying the human body composition and its changes with increasing age, to achieve timely
diagnosis of these pathologies.

title: Characterizing the role of MSRA in pancreatic tumorigenesis
text:
The current proposal “Characterizing the role of MSRA in pancreatic tumorigenesis” will use organoid models,
chemical proteomics, and biochemical tools to elucidate fundamental aspects of redox metabolism in
pancreatic cancer. We anticipate our results will establish mechanistic understanding and therapeutic inroads
for methionine-based redox signaling in pancreatic cancer.

title: Computational methods for learning B cell differentiation networks
text:
During the course of adaptive immune responses, naive B cells are activated and undergo a
series of cell fate choices including the possibility of becoming long-lived plasma cells that secrete
antibodies to provide lasting protection from recurrent infection. This project will integrate
phylogenetic and transcriptional trajectory-based computational methods to analyze high-
throughput single cell antibody receptor and transcriptomic data to define the regulatory logic
underlying differential fate decisions and link the multiple stages of B cell differentiation.
Application of these methods to human immune profiling data will serve as method validation and
the knowledge gained may provide a basis for designing more effective vaccines or
immunotherapies.

title: Discerning L-type trafficking modulation by targeted excision of ubiquitin and SUMO
text:
A better understanding of normal cardiac physiology and pathophysiology is necessary to develop novel
therapeutics against heart disease, which is the leading cause of mortality in the United States. Heart rhythm
relies on the faithful positioning of L-type channels at heart cell surface as derangement is linked to severe
disorders including ventricular arrythmias and heart failure. The proposed research will elucidate molecular
mechanisms underlying surface trafficking and functional regulation of cardiac L-type channels, and bridge
mechanistic insights to advance the development of targeted therapeutics for heart diseases.

title: Deep Learning and Subtyping of Post-COVID-19 Lung Progression Phenotypes
text:
RELEVANCE TO PUBLIC HEALTH
This study seeks to understand the long-term consequences to lung function in patients who recover from the
novel coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). The proposed deep learning algorithms will utilize chest X-ray and
computed tomography images to identify post-COVID-19 progression subtypes and establish their associations
with distinct clinical, imaging and mechanistic biomarkers. The knowledge gained from this study will improve
the management and treatment of post-COVID-19 patients.

title: Discovery and functional analysis of novel candidate genes and variants underlying craniofacial diversification in Cyprinodon pupfishes
text:
PUBLIC HEALTH RELEVANCE: The proposed research will provide fundamental knowledge about how genes
control craniofacial development in vertebrates. This knowledge will help develop therapeutic targets and
treatments for human craniofacial diseases. Since the majority of birth defects are craniofacial and dental
abnormalities, this research will lead to improved diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of human birth defects.

title: Epigenetic sex determinants of cardiometabolic disease and prevention
text:
PROJECT 1: Epigenetic sex determinants of cardiometabolic disease and prevention
NARRATIVE
Women and men differ in the development of cardiovascular disease risk factors such as obesity, and women
are more likely than men to experience adverse effects from statin drugs. We have identified genes on the X
and Y chromosomes that work in conjunction with hormones such as estrogen and testosterone to influence
obesity and vulnerability to statin drug side effects. A better understanding of how these X and Y chromosome
genes regulate obesity and drug response will contribute to development of therapies that optimally benefit
both women and men.

title: Development and Testing of a Mechanism-Driven Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) Skills Coaching Powered by Generative AI: A Just-in-Time Adaptive Intervention to Reduce HIV and Substance Use Risks
text:
People who use substances face disproportionately high risks for HIV infection due to impulsivity, maladaptive
coping, and limited engagement in prevention services such as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). The goals of
this project are 1) to develop a generative AI-enhanced dialectical behavior therapy skills coaching delivered
using a just-in-time adaptive intervention, and 2) to evaluate its feasibility and safety among HIV-negative
substance-using adults. By delivering personalized support at moments of behavioral risk, this intervention
aims to reduce substance use and HIV transmission and lay the groundwork for scalable AI-driven tools
addressing a range of behavioral health challenges.

title: Evaluation of the prevalence of xylazine and etiology of xylazine related invasive infections
text:
Xylazine, an alpha 2 adrenergic receptor agonist with sedative and analgesic properties is rapidly infiltrating
the United States illegal drug supply. Recent case series and reports from hospitals at the epicenter of this
emerging epidemic have identified an overwhelming number of invasive infections, particularly cutaneous
ulcers and necrotizing skin and soft tissue infections in people who use xylazine. This grant application will
provide information on the types of illicit drugs contaminated with xylazine as well as microbiologic data on the
types of pathogens contaminating xylazine adulterated drugs and causing severe infections in people who use
xylazine.

title: Validation of imaging brain tumor metabolism using deuterated glucose
text:
In this project we search to validate the use of a new type of MRI technique, called Deuterium Metabolic Imaging
(DMI) as a tool to detect abnormal glucose metabolism in brain tumors. We test the new technology by comparing
with existing methods for validation, and also to reveal any improved performance. In addition, the use of DMI is
evaluated as technique to detect early treatment effects in brain tumors.

title: CSHL Conference on Probabilistic Modeling in Genomics
text: The explosion of genomic information in the past decade poses an enormous challenge to computational biologists. These data are highly informative, massive in scale, yet often noisy and difficult to interpret. Sophisticated statistical and machine-learning tools are needed to make sense of them and draw useful conclusions about biological processes as they unfold in time and space. The Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory conference on Probabilistic Modelling in Genomes will focus on all aspects of modeling and inference as it applies to genomic data, spanning applications in disease, complex traits, gene expression, and evolution. The goal of the series is explore the latest modeling techniques, mathematical and computational tools, and algorithmic approaches for interpretation of complex genomic data sets.

title: Evaluation of Trigeminal Ganglia Sensory Neuronal Population/s Mediating MIF-Induced Anti-Nociception in a Model of Apical Periodontitis.
text:
Persistent dental pain after treatment of apical periodontitis has a major clinical impact, however, currently
available drugs have adverse effects, potential for physical dependency, and provide incomplete pain relief. We
propose to study the neuronal subpopulation that stem cell released macrophage migratory inhibitory factors
targets to mediate pain relief in a model of apical periodontitis. The proposed studies will advance the study of a
targeted therapeutic to treat millions experiencing persistent dental pain.

title: Development of tools for analyzing cell-cell communication using spatial transcriptomic data
text:
Cell-cell communication is one of the most fundamental, yet poorly understood problems in modern biology. The
proposed work will combine mathematical modeling and machine learning to develop analysis tools for
systematic screening of cell-cell communication using spatial transcriptomic data. The results will be directly
relevant to understanding of tissue organization in space, the mechanisms of microenvironment for tumors,
developmental processes, and cell fate decision.

title: Understanding the role of catheter-associated protein deposition in the development of CAUTI
text:
Urinary catheterization is one of the most common healthcare-related procedures; however, placement of a
catheter is known to predispose patients to the development of catheter-associated urinary tract infections.
Bladder inflammation is induced upon catheterization and changing the bladder environment allowing a diverse
group of pathogens to infect. Fibrinogen, a proinflammatory protein, is released in the bladder and deposited
onto the catheter surface, becoming a key platform for microbial colonization. This project focuses on
understanding how modulation of protein deposition on the catheter by using a liquid surface coating may affect
microbial colonization, biofilm formation, and systemic dissemination, as well as the inflammation response. This
approach will offer new insights to inform the development of new clinical treatments that will continue to remain
effective long-term.

title: Interpretable Machine Intelligence for Biomarker Discovery in Concussion
text:
This proposal aims to advance traumatic brain injury (TBI) research, focusing on mild TBI (mTBI) among service
members and veterans. Utilizing advanced multidimensional statistical methodologies, we aim to uncover novel
biomarker panels corresponding to distinct clinical outcomes. The first objective involves applying a novel
machine learning workflow, integrating non-linear principal component analysis (NLPCA) with supervised
classifiers, to analyze biomarker data from the LIMBIC-CENC database to aid in identifying protein panels linked
to enduring functional impairments in Veterans with mTBI. The second objective focuses on conducting a
comprehensive proteomic analysis to identify unique patient subgroups and their associated protein signatures.
The final objective includes testing these biomarker panels with the independent TRACTS dataset for validation
and identifying signatures unique to long term clinical outcomes.
